video.title: Sell These $3.5K AI Pitch Decks Built in 12 Min (+4 More Ideas)

summary: Chris Koerner and Nick discuss ways to turn AI tools into services, lead magnets, and software, with AI-generated pitch decks as the central example. They brainstorm a gated community for sharing AI use cases, quizzes for AI recommendations and hiring, automated deck redesigns, and AI-generated market reports. Most concepts are early-stage or hypothetical; the video gives more detail on workflows and possible customer acquisition than on proven revenue. A recurring theme is to use AI to synthesize information and produce useful starting points, then have people refine the result.

speakers.name: Nick
speakers.description: Addressed as Nick; the transcript does not establish his surname.

ideas.name: AI-generated pitch decks for newly launched funds
ideas.one_liner: Find new funds in SEC filings, generate a tailored pitch deck, and offer it to the fund manager.
ideas.business_model: One-off pitch deck sales, with AI-assisted production and outbound prospecting.
ideas.customer: People launching investment funds, including funds buying single-family homes.
ideas.problem: New funds need a polished deck to explain their investment proposition.
ideas.offer: Create a pitch deck using fund information and examples of the desired design; the automated outreach concept offers the first five slides before asking the prospect to buy.

price_points.label: Price attributed to the pitch deck guy

pricing.notes: The $3,500 price is reported about another operator, not claimed as the speakers' own price.

acquisition_channels.details: The pitch deck operator reportedly scrapes SEC filings for newly launched funds and emails prospects at the right time with a portfolio. The proposed automation would email a watermarked deck and offer the first five slides. UK automation should target corporate subscribers and verify recipient type and consent requirements.

quote.text: he will do cold outreach to them in the right time, the right moment, and say, "Hey, I saw you launched a fund for buying single family homes. Congratulations. I'd love to make a pitch deck for you. Here's my portfolio."
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.delivery: A person or AI agent gathers fund information and creates a PowerPoint deck. The proposed workflow sends source information and design examples to Manus through its API, then returns a watermarked deck to the prospect. A human would likely need to check accuracy and visual quality before sale.
unit_economics_claims: A pitch deck operator reportedly charges $3,500 per deck.

acquisition.how: SEC filing monitoring and corporate contact research could be automated. Cold email to limited companies can be automated with checks; the target's legal status and message compliance need review.

onboarding.how: An agent could collect public fund details and request missing information, with a human checking the brief.

delivery.how: An API could create a draft deck from fund data and design examples; a human should review claims, source accuracy, and slide quality.

billing.how: A checkout and file-delivery workflow could collect payment and release the finished deck after approval.

support.how: Agents could answer routine questions, but revisions and bespoke design requests would need human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: The service can target UK funds and use UK company filings, but the transcript's prospecting example relies on SEC filings and US funds. Adapt the research source and check UK electronic-marketing rules for each recipient.

risks: Generated decks may contain inaccurate financial or market claims, so a human must verify the content.
The process depends on identifying a fund at the right launch moment and finding an appropriate contact.
Automated cold outreach to individuals or sole traders may breach UK PECR; confirm the recipient is a corporate subscriber and handle personal data appropriately.
The transcript notes uncertainty about how Manus handles data.

ideas.name: Gated community for sharing AI use cases
ideas.one_liner: Let people share an AI use case before browsing and voting on other submissions, then email the most popular ideas.
ideas.business_model: Potential newsletter and audience business; monetisation beyond email subscriptions is not stated.
ideas.customer: People who want practical ideas for using AI in their work or personal lives.
ideas.problem: People find it difficult to decide how to apply AI and which tools to start with.
ideas.offer: A website where visitors submit an AI use case to unlock other submissions, upvote ideas, and optionally subscribe to a weekly email of the top-voted ideas.

pricing.notes: The transcript discusses email capture, not a stated price.

acquisition_channels.details: The domain was chosen after looking up the phrase in Google Trends, but a search strategy or organic traffic plan is not stated.
The idea arose from an existing podcast conversation about how people use AI. A launch or audience promotion plan is not stated.

ideas.delivery: A website accepts a text submission, unlocks the use-case list and voting, and collects email addresses for a weekly newsletter. Replit was building the initial website during the discussion.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the speaker says he bought the domain, but gives no cost.

acquisition.how: Search traffic and sharing could bring submissions automatically after launch; no acquisition system is described.

onboarding.how: A form can collect use cases and email addresses, then unlock the site automatically.

delivery.how: Software can display submissions, collect votes, rank ideas, and send a weekly digest, with moderation checks for spam and quality.

billing.how: No paid product is specified; paid newsletter billing would need to be added if introduced.

support.how: Automated help can cover account and submission questions, while abuse reports and moderation need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: A web community and email newsletter can operate in the UK. Collecting emails requires appropriate privacy and marketing consent practices.

risks: The idea was only minutes old in the discussion and had no validation or revenue evidence.
Gating all content behind a submission could discourage visitors or lead to low-quality submissions.
The value depends on steady, useful contributions and moderation.

ideas.name: AI model recommendation quiz
ideas.one_liner: Use a quiz to recommend which AI model and implementation approach best fits a business owner.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; the example gates the result behind an email address and could generate leads.
ideas.customer: Entrepreneurs or business owners trying to choose an AI model for their needs.
ideas.problem: Users may not know which AI tool fits their goals, skills, or intended use.
ideas.offer: An online quiz asks about a user's business goals and comfort with technology, then recommends an AI model and implementation approach.

pricing.notes: The example asks for an email to reveal the quiz score; no paid offer is described.

acquisition_channels.details: The quiz uses insights from podcast interviews, but the transcript does not state how it was promoted or how many users took it.

ideas.delivery: The creator gathered interview data, asked an LLM to help create a quiz, built it in Lovable, and gated results behind an email address. The LLM generates a result profile and explanation.
unit_economics_claims: The creator says the first version took a couple of hours and that a repeat build would take about an hour.

acquisition.how: A quiz can be shared through an existing audience or search traffic, but the transcript gives no tested acquisition process.

onboarding.how: The quiz collects answers and an email address through a form.

delivery.how: An LLM can score answers and generate a recommendation, with periodic human checks for accuracy.

billing.how: No billing is described; payment could be added if the quiz becomes a paid product.

support.how: Automated FAQs could handle basic questions, while disputed or confusing recommendations need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: A software recommendation quiz can serve UK businesses. The quiz would need accurate, current information about the models it recommends.

risks: The quiz result is a general recommendation and may not reflect a user's complete needs.
Model features and products change, so the quiz needs regular review.
Email gating may reduce completion and requires clear consent for follow-up marketing.

ideas.name: Personality-based job matching and placement
ideas.one_liner: Match employers and job seekers using quizzes that describe company culture and candidate preferences.
ideas.business_model: Potential placement fees, job-board services, or employer subscriptions; only a recruiter placement comparison is discussed.
ideas.customer: Employers and job seekers, especially companies that value culture fit and want compatible applicants.
ideas.problem: Employers may lose candidates because of poor culture fit even when candidates can be trained for the role.
ideas.offer: Create a company profile from a culture quiz, assess job seekers with a related quiz, then show employers candidates with similar scores or preferences.

pricing.model: Potential recruiter-style placement fee; no price for the proposed service is set.
pricing.notes: The speakers discuss recruiter fees as a comparison, not as a validated price for this product.

acquisition_channels.details: The proposed approach is to contact HR and hiring people on LinkedIn and offer a company culture quiz. Automated unsolicited messages to individuals may be restricted under UK electronic-marketing rules.

The speakers describe collecting candidate emails through quizzes and notifying hiring managers about matches. UK cold email automation should be limited to eligible corporate subscribers and checked for compliance.
A company or creator could use an existing following to promote a hiring quiz and build a candidate list.

ideas.delivery: Employers and job seekers complete separate quizzes. Software calculates or compares profiles and notifies hiring managers of candidates with matching scores. Human recruiters or hiring managers would still make placement and hiring decisions.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers compare the idea with recruiter fees of 10% to 30% of first-year salary.
A $150,000 salary and a $10,000 placement fee are used as an example.
A quiz might take 10 to 20 minutes to complete.
A creator with 800,000 to 1 million views and 1% completion could gather 8,000 to 10,000 email-address submissions.

acquisition.how: The suggested direct LinkedIn outreach targets individual HR staff and job seekers; automated unsolicited messages may not be lawful in the UK. Inbound employer and candidate acquisition could score higher.

onboarding.how: Forms can collect employer and candidate preferences and build profiles automatically, with checks for misleading or incomplete answers.

delivery.how: Software can compare quiz results and notify employers; human review is needed to assess suitability and make hiring decisions.

billing.how: Placement or subscription billing could be automated, but the proposed pricing and terms are not established.

support.how: Automated support can handle quiz and profile questions, while disputes, accessibility needs, and hiring concerns require people.

uk_applicability.notes: The model can operate in the UK, but hiring assessments and personal data handling need careful review. The suggested automated outreach to individuals also raises PECR compliance concerns.

risks: Personality quizzes may be biased, easy to game, or weak predictors of job performance.
Employers could mistake a compatibility score for a reliable hiring assessment.
Handling candidate data requires clear privacy, retention, and access controls.
Automated unsolicited LinkedIn messages or emails to individuals may breach UK rules.

ideas.name: Company-specific culture quiz for recruiting
ideas.one_liner: Help a company make a custom hiring quiz that captures its culture and builds a list of potential candidates.
ideas.business_model: Not stated; the quiz is described as a company lead magnet and internal recruiting tool.
ideas.customer: Companies that want to attract and identify people likely to fit their culture.
ideas.problem: A company may struggle to explain its culture or find candidates who prefer its working style.
ideas.offer: Create a custom quiz from company data and interview preferences; let candidates take it in exchange for their email and use results to search a candidate list when a role opens.

pricing.notes: The transcript describes an internal tool and lead magnet, not a paid service price.

acquisition_channels.details: The speakers suggest that a company or creator could promote its quiz to followers and collect candidate emails.
The quiz itself is proposed as a lead magnet that attracts job seekers; no other tested channel is stated.

ideas.delivery: An LLM uses company information and interview preferences to generate a quiz. Candidates complete it and submit an email to receive results; the employer searches the resulting list when a role opens.
unit_economics_claims: A 20-minute build is given as an example for a quiz promoted by a creator.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the example is an internal recruiting tool and lead magnet.

acquisition.how: An employer can promote the quiz through its own audience and hiring pages; direct automated messaging to individuals needs UK compliance review.

onboarding.how: Candidate answers and email capture can be handled by a form.

delivery.how: An LLM can generate a draft quiz and software can score responses, but humans should validate questions and evaluate applicants.

support.how: Automated help can answer basic quiz questions, while candidate concerns and hiring decisions need human handling.

uk_applicability.notes: Custom recruiting quizzes can be used by UK employers, but candidate data, fairness, accessibility, and employment law need careful handling.

risks: A quiz can create unfair or discriminatory filters if questions or scoring encode unsuitable preferences.
Candidate email collection needs a clear purpose, privacy notice, and retention policy.
A large list does not guarantee qualified applicants or a successful hire.

quotes.text: It's a lead magnet. People start taking it and then they're just they're just building in order to get the quiz results, you've got to put your email in.

ideas.name: Automated redesign of uploaded slide decks
ideas.one_liner: Find public slide decks, redesign them with AI, and offer the improved version back to the original creator.
ideas.customer: People or organisations that upload decks to SlideShare.
ideas.problem: Existing presentations may be useful but visually dated or poorly designed.
ideas.offer: Redesign a public deck and send the creator a preview, then charge if they want to use the improved version.

pricing.notes: The speakers give these as possible prices, not proven sales.

acquisition_channels.details: Monitor decks uploaded to SlideShare, redesign them, then contact the original creator with a preview. Check platform terms and rights before reuse or outreach.

ideas.delivery: An automated workflow detects a deck, uses AI to redesign it, and sends a preview to the original creator. Human review should check the deck and ensure the source material can be reused.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers suggest charging $20 or $200 for a redesigned deck.

acquisition.how: Finding public uploads can be automated, but unsolicited messages to individual creators may not be allowed in the UK without consent.

onboarding.how: A creator could approve the source deck and choose a style through a form, but the proposal does not define this flow.

delivery.how: AI can create a redesign draft; a human should check the content, rights, and final design.

billing.how: Checkout and digital file delivery could be automated after a creator approves the preview.

support.how: Agents can answer basic purchase questions, but custom revisions and rights concerns need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The service could target UK creators, but platform terms, copyright, and UK marketing rules affect automated discovery and outreach.

risks: Redesigning a deck without permission could infringe copyright or violate platform terms.
Automated unsolicited direct messages to individual creators raise UK PECR concerns.
Creators may not value or trust a redesign they did not request.

quotes.text: create a permissionless thing that anytime a new slide is uploaded to Slides Share, you revamp it, you redesign it

quotes.text: If you do, buy it for 20 bucks, 200 bucks, whatever, and automate it and automate it.

ideas.problem: A lesson plan may be more useful or appealing when accompanied by presentation slides.
ideas.offer: Create a pitch deck or slide presentation to accompany a lesson plan and offer it as a paid add-on or bundle.

pricing.model: Possible one-off conversion fee; the quoted $20 or $200 range is suggested for deck redesign generally.
pricing.notes: No specific price for teacher lesson-plan decks is stated.

acquisition_channels.details: Identify teachers selling lesson plans on Teachers Pay Teachers and propose adding a deck. The transcript suggests mass direct messages; unsolicited marketing to individual teachers may be restricted under UK PECR.

ideas.delivery: An AI tool turns a lesson plan or outline into a presentation. A person should check the lesson content and suitability before it is sold.

acquisition.how: Marketplace discovery could be automated, but the proposed mass direct messaging targets individual sellers and is unsuitable for automated UK marketing without consent.

onboarding.how: A seller could submit a lesson plan and specify a presentation style through a form.

delivery.how: AI can draft slides from a plan, but a teacher should check accuracy, age suitability, and teaching quality.

billing.how: A digital marketplace can collect payment and deliver a file automatically if sellers and buyers agree to the arrangement.

support.how: Automated support can cover file access; content corrections and marketplace disputes need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: The digital service could be adapted for UK teachers, though the named marketplace and its audience are US-oriented and curriculum content must be localised.

risks: The named marketplace may have rules against unsolicited seller contact or derivative products.
Lesson content must be accurate, age-appropriate, and aligned with the relevant curriculum.
Automated direct messages to individual teachers may breach UK marketing rules.

ideas.name: AI-generated market research reports for decision makers
ideas.one_liner: Use an AI research tool to assemble sourced market information into reports that help business decision makers.
ideas.business_model: Potential research service or consulting support for decision makers; no price is set.
ideas.customer: Business owners, consultants, and decision makers who need market information to make choices.
ideas.problem: Researching market size, competitors, pricing, downloads, revenue, and customer trends takes time.
ideas.offer: Generate a researched report with charts, summaries, and downloadable files using an AI research platform.

pricing.notes: A $2,000 report is discussed as an IBISWorld comparison, not as a price for this proposed service.

acquisition_channels.details: The speakers suggest a business built around serving decision makers with research. A concrete customer acquisition channel is not stated.

ideas.delivery: Perplexity Labs can research a prompt and present information through text, charts, PDFs, or CSV files with sources. A human should validate the data and conclusions before clients rely on them.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers say a Perplexity plan costs $20 per month.
They cite IBISWorld charging $2,000 for reports as a comparison.
A keto-app market research task is said to return results in 11 minutes and include 37 sources.
ideas.startup_cost: The speakers state a Perplexity plan costs $20 per month; other startup costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: No proven acquisition method is described. Inbound content and a research portfolio could automate discovery, while selling to larger businesses would need human relationship work.

onboarding.how: A form could collect a research brief, though a human should clarify scope and verify that the question is answerable.

delivery.how: The platform can assemble research and visual outputs; human checks are needed for source quality, data accuracy, and interpretation.

billing.how: A fixed report fee could be collected through checkout, but the transcript does not describe payment operations.

support.how: Agents can explain report contents, but questions about sources and business implications need human review.

uk_applicability.notes: Market research is applicable to UK businesses, but the examples focus on US data and may need UK sources, currency, and market-specific validation.

risks: AI-generated research may contain inaccurate, stale, or weakly supported data.
Charts can imply correlations that do not establish causation.
Clients may rely on unsupported claims when making consequential decisions.
The video does not show a paid customer or demonstrated willingness to pay for these reports.

quotes.text: So to me, it would be a business built around servicing decision makers, people who who have high leverage positions that are making decisions all day.

ideas.name: Industry research report as an agency lead magnet
ideas.one_liner: Give a target business a tailored industry report to start a sales conversation for an agency or consultancy.
ideas.business_model: Agency or consulting services acquired through a free research report; paid service pricing is not stated.
ideas.customer: Digital agencies, consultants, and B2B suppliers seeking business customers.
ideas.problem: Agencies need a useful reason to start a conversation with prospects and build trust.
ideas.offer: Generate a specific market report for a prospect's industry and send it as a lead magnet, then follow up about the agency's service.

pricing.model: Not stated; the report is positioned as a free lead magnet for a separate agency service.
pricing.notes: The $2,000 report price mentioned is an external comparison, not a stated agency price.

acquisition_channels.details: The proposed tactic is to send a tailored report to target companies and follow up later. UK cold email should be restricted to eligible corporate subscribers and compliant contact data.

ideas.delivery: An agency uses Perplexity Labs to build a report from available market data, sends it as a useful prospecting asset, tracks whether the recipient opens it, and follows up. A person should validate claims before sending.
unit_economics_claims: The speakers compare such a report with reports that IBISWorld reportedly sells for $2,000.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the speakers mention a $20 per month Perplexity plan elsewhere.

acquisition.how: Research and contact-list preparation can be automated, but the suggested email follow-up must meet UK rules and should be reviewed for relevance.

onboarding.how: No paying client onboarding is described; an agency would need a human to scope any follow-on work.

delivery.how: AI can draft the report and charts, but a human should check the sources, conclusions, and prospect-specific details.

billing.how: The lead magnet is free; billing for later agency work is not described.

support.how: An agent could handle simple follow-ups, but interpreting the report and discussing consulting work would need human involvement.

uk_applicability.notes: A UK agency can use tailored research to open B2B conversations, but must use appropriate UK data sources and comply with PECR when emailing prospects.

risks: The report may be inaccurate or irrelevant, damaging trust instead of building it.
Open tracking and follow-up must be handled consistently with privacy and marketing rules.
This is a lead-generation tactic, not evidence that prospects will buy the agency's services.
